A digital garden is a collection of linked notes that stay open to revision. A note can begin with a question or an excerpt. Later, it can acquire an explanation, a worked example, or a correction. Keeping these changes on the same page gives the idea an address that other notes can refer to. Maggie Appleton’s account describes this practice of publishing unfinished work and revisiting it.
The links make this a form of hypertext. They also need context: a sentence around a link can say whether its target supplies a definition, evidence, or an objection. Wikipedia is a familiar example of linked, revisable pages. A personal garden leaves the selection and interpretation with its author.
Ted Nelson’s Xanadu has further requirements, including durable connections to quoted material and a system for paying rightsholders. Calling any collection of linked notes a Xanadu system would skip those commitments. Nelson’s own explanation draws out the distinction.
Joel Hooks describes the maintenance implied by the name:

A garden is usually a place where things grow.
Gardens can be very personal and full of whimsy or a garden can be a source of food and substance.
We gather and work together in community gardens to share the labor as well as the rewards of a collective effort.
It’s a comparison that you can take very far. From “planting seeds” and “pulling weeds” to tending multiple gardens that each serve an individual need or desired outcome.
Like with real gardens, our digital gardens are a constant ebb and flow towards entropy.

See also: Tom Critchlow’s Building a digital garden.
The garden and the stream
Mike Caulfield uses the stream for posts arranged by time and the garden for ideas arranged through their connections. A stream records an unfolding conversation. A garden gives a topic a page that can collect evidence from several conversations and be revised when that evidence changes.
His example starts with a news story and becomes a page about a claim in the underlying study. Adding a related note exposes a possible confounder in his first interpretation. That is a concrete use for the links: following one can change what the current page should say.

I don’t want people to get hung up on the technology angle. I think sometimes people hear “Federated Thingamabob” and just sort of tune out thinking “Oh, he’s talking about a feature of Federated Thingamabob.” But I’m not. I’m really not. I’m talking about a different way to think your online activity, no matter what tool you use. And relevant to this conference, I’m talking about a different way of collaborating as well.
